explanations.explanation: The messengers tell Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, “A vast army is coming against you from Edom, from beyond the Sea…” (2 Chronicles 20:2). They add that it's already in Hazazon-tamar, which is En-gedi. So this isn't a rumor from far away. It's practically at the door. I'd have burned a whole batch just hearing that news.

Egypt does show up later in the king's prayer, but only as the land Israel came out of (2 Chronicles 20:10). The messengers tell Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, that this army is coming from Edom, from beyond the Sea. They also say it's already in Hazazon-tamar, which is En-gedi. The text never mentions the Nile here.

Assyria never comes up in this part of the story. The men who warn Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, name Edom, from beyond the Sea. They also say the army is already in Hazazon-tamar, which is En-gedi. That's a lot closer than a far-off river, friend.

explanations.answer: He sets his face to seek the LORD
explanations.explanation: The text says Jehoshaphat was alarmed, and right after that he “set his face to seek the LORD.” Alarmed, but he still turned toward God first. He didn't stop at a plan. He went looking for God. That's a king who knows where to run first.

explanations.answer: He calls up every soldier in Judah
explanations.explanation: The text never says Jehoshaphat calls up a single soldier here. It says he was alarmed, set his face to seek the LORD, and proclaimed a fast throughout Judah. The first move was toward God, not toward the barracks. I know that's not the answer most people would expect from a king.

explanations.answer: He sends gold to buy them off
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text has Jehoshaphat sending gold to anybody. What it says is that he was alarmed and set his face to seek the LORD. Then he proclaimed a fast throughout Judah. If it had been me, I'd have tried a free cookie box and a firm handshake, and the text tells us a far better move.
After he sets his face to seek the LORD, Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast throughout Judah. The whole land is told to do this together. Every person in Judah has a reason to look up, not just the king.

A census counts heads, and the text never says anyone gets counted here. Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast throughout Judah. Counting the people wouldn't have told him much, since he already knew a vast army was coming.

A festival would be a party, and nobody in Judah is in a party mood here. The king was alarmed. So he proclaims a fast throughout Judah, and then the people gather to seek the LORD. Save the party hats for later, friend.

This one's false. The text says the people of Judah gathered to seek the LORD, and they came “from all the cities of Judah to seek Him.” That's way more than one city. Judah showed up from everywhere.

The text says the people of Judah gathered to seek the LORD, and they came “from all the cities of Judah to seek Him.” It's a whole kingdom, not one crowd from the capital. Think of every road in Judah filling up at once. That's a lot of feet headed toward one place.

Jehoshaphat prays that God gave this land forever to the descendants of Abraham, His friend. He's reminding God of an old promise, right there in front of the assembly. He's praying with his memory open. I think that's a smart way to start when you're scared.

Moses, Israel's leader, doesn't show up in this part of the prayer. Jehoshaphat names Abraham, God's friend, as the one whose descendants got the land forever. Moses was a great leader, but the prayer goes back even further to Abraham.

David, Israel's king, isn't the name in this prayer. Jehoshaphat says God gave the land forever to the descendants of Abraham, whom he calls God's friend. That's the name the king reaches back for. It's a long way back, but the promise reaches that far too.

Jehoshaphat repeats what the people said when they built the sanctuary: when they cried out in distress, “You will hear us and save us.” That's what they were counting on. He's holding that sentence up in prayer right now. Hear and save, friend, that's the whole answer.

A new king never comes up in what the people said. They said they'd stand before the temple and cry out in distress, and God would hear them and save them. They already have a king, and he's the one praying. Hear and save is the promise.

A bigger army isn't what they said. They said they'd cry out to God in distress, and He would hear them and save them. Jehoshaphat will soon say they're powerless before this army anyway. So he's not asking for more soldiers.

That's not what the king says. He says, “See how they are repaying us by coming to drive us out of the possession that You gave us as an inheritance.” They're coming to push Judah out, not to make peace. Nobody shows up with a peace offering when the plan is to take your land.

Jehoshaphat says it plainly: “See how they are repaying us by coming to drive us out of the possession that You gave us as an inheritance.” Peace is the opposite of what he's describing. He's laying out the real problem to God, with nothing hidden.

explanations.answer: They don't know what to do but their eyes are on God
explanations.explanation: After saying they're powerless, Jehoshaphat says, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You.” A king with no plan and nothing to hide. I think that's one of the bravest sentences in this whole story. He's not out of hope, he just knows where to look.

explanations.answer: They will fight on until the very last man falls
explanations.explanation: That's a speech from a different story. Jehoshaphat has just said they are powerless, so he isn't making a big fighting promise. He says, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You.” It's a prayer, not a battle cry.

explanations.answer: They will send to Egypt for horses and chariots
explanations.explanation: The king never mentions sending to Egypt for horses or chariots. After admitting they are powerless, he says, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You.” He doesn't look around for outside help. He looks up.

The text says all the men of Judah, “with their wives and children and little ones,” were standing before the LORD. It's the whole community, not just the leaders. Nobody's watching this from the sidelines. They're all there together.
The text says all the men of Judah were standing before the LORD, “with their wives and children and little ones.” It's the whole community together, not just the men. Even the little ones are there.

Jahaziel, a Levite from Asaph's descendants, speaks after the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him. He says, “…the battle does not belong to you, but to God.” That takes the weight off the king and the whole crowd. They don't have to carry it.

That's the opposite of the message. Jahaziel, a Levite from Asaph's descendants, says, “…the battle does not belong to you, but to God.” Even the king gets told the battle isn't his. Jehoshaphat just finished admitting he was powerless, so that's good news.

Jahaziel is a Levite himself, but he doesn't claim the battle for his own group. He says, “…the battle does not belong to you, but to God.” The Spirit of the LORD came upon him to say it. So nobody in the room owns this fight.

explanations.answer: Stand firm and see the LORD save them
explanations.explanation: Jahaziel says, “Take up your positions, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf…” They show up, stand firm and watch God save them. He also says, “You need not fight this battle.” Their job is to be there and trust.

explanations.answer: Fight hard and drive the army back
explanations.explanation: The message is closer to the opposite. Jahaziel says, “You need not fight this battle.” They're told to take their positions, stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD. Driving anyone back isn't on their list.

explanations.answer: Surround the camp and strike at night
explanations.explanation: No night raid is planned here. Jahaziel tells them where the army will be tomorrow, then says, “You need not fight this battle.” Their part is to take their positions, stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD. It's the quietest battle plan I've ever heard.

explanations.answer: Believe in the LORD and His prophets
explanations.explanation: As they set out, Jehoshaphat says, “Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld; believe in His prophets, and you will succeed.” He sends them off with trust, not a pep talk about swords. They've just heard a prophet speak, so he's pointing right back to that word.

explanations.answer: Keep their swords ready the whole way
explanations.explanation: Swords aren't what Jehoshaphat brings up. He says, “Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld; believe in His prophets, and you will succeed.” Jahaziel already said they need not fight this battle. So the king points them to belief.

explanations.answer: Turn back if their hearts are afraid
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets told to turn back. Jahaziel said, “Do not be afraid or discouraged. Go out and face them tomorrow…” and Jehoshaphat adds, “Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld…” The whole message is about going forward on trust.

Jehoshaphat appoints those who would sing to the LORD and praise the splendor of His holiness. They go out before the army singing, “Give thanks to the LORD, for His loving devotion endures forever.” That's what's leading the way. Not one weapon in the lead.

The text doesn't mention a single archer. Jehoshaphat appoints singers to go out before the army, to sing to the LORD and praise the splendor of His holiness. A choir takes the lead, which is not what any army manual would say.
The ark isn't mentioned anywhere in this march. Jehoshaphat consults with the people and appoints singers to go out before the army. They sing to the LORD and praise the splendor of His holiness.

The text says, “The moment they began their shouts and praises, the LORD set ambushes against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir…” The timing is right there in the verse. The praise starts, and the LORD acts. Judah is still singing, and the battle is already being handled.

explanations.answer: He sends hailstones down on them
explanations.explanation: Hailstones aren't in this story. The text says the LORD set ambushes against the men of Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir the moment the shouts and praises began. Stick with what the passage says. It's plenty dramatic already.

explanations.answer: He sends hornets out against them
explanations.explanation: No hornets here, friend. The text says that the moment they began their shouts and praises, the LORD set ambushes against the men of Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir. They were defeated. That's the exact word the passage uses.

It goes the other way. Once they finished off the inhabitants of Seir, the Ammonites and Moabites “helped to destroy one another.” There's no peace treaty in this verse. And Judah is still on the march, watching none of it.

The text says that when they finished off the inhabitants of Seir, the Ammonites and Moabites “helped to destroy one another.” They turned on each other instead of making peace. It's a hard verse. And all of it happens while Judah is still on its way.

explanations.answer: Only bodies lying on the ground
explanations.explanation: The men of Judah come to a place overlooking the wilderness and look for the vast army. What they find is “only corpses lying on the ground; no one had escaped.” This part is heavy. The army they were afraid of isn't there anymore.

explanations.answer: The army lined up for battle
explanations.explanation: There's no army standing in rows. The men of Judah look for the vast army and see “only corpses lying on the ground; no one had escaped.” That's a heavy verse. The battle was already over before Judah got there.

explanations.answer: An empty camp and fresh tracks
explanations.explanation: Nobody slipped away leaving tracks. The text says there were “only corpses lying on the ground; no one had escaped.” It's a heavy moment. The vast army was gone, and Judah had only to look.

Judah gathers plunder for three days because there's so much of it. They found more than they could carry away. Then on the fourth day they assembled to bless the LORD. Three whole days of hauling, friend, and I'd want a nap by lunch.

Seven isn't the number here. The text says they were gathering the plunder for three days because there was so much. Even after three days, it was more than they could carry. That's already a long stretch of hauling.
Forty is way too many. The text says Judah gathered the plunder for three days because there was so much. They found more than they could carry away. Forty days of hauling would need a very big box.

On the fourth day, they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, where they blessed the LORD. After three days of gathering plunder, they stop and turn back to Him. The place was still called the Valley of Beracah when this was written.

The text says it plainly: on the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, where they blessed the LORD. After three days of gathering, they stop to bless Him. That's the place the passage says is still called by that name.

They entered Jerusalem and went into the house of the LORD “with harps, lyres, and trumpets.” They came back joyful, and the music came with them. The march that started with singers ends with instruments.

The text says they entered Jerusalem and went into the house of the LORD “with harps, lyres, and trumpets.” They came home with joy and with music. It was a loud parade, and I think it was a good one.

The text says, “the fear of God came upon all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel.” Word travels fast. Every kingdom around hears what the LORD did.

Anger isn't the word here. The text says the fear of God came upon all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel. The nations didn't storm back. They heard what God had done.

Favor isn't what the text says. The fear of God came upon all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel. That's a very different reaction than warm feelings.

explanations.answer: At peace with rest on every side
explanations.explanation: The text says Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace, “for his God had given him rest on every side.” After all that fear, rest. The peace came from God, and it covered every side. Quiet like that is hard to bake.
No famine here. The text says Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace, for his God had given him rest on every side. That's the opposite of trouble. After a day like that one, rest was the right ending.
Nobody's paying tribute in this verse. The text says Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace, for his God had given him rest on every side. Judah was resting, not paying anyone.

Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah, a prophet, says, “Because you have allied yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works.” Ahaziah was king of Israel, and the text says he acted wickedly. The reason is right there in the prophet's own words. It's a sad ending after such a great victory.

explanations.answer: Jehoshaphat built ships without asking God
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that reason. Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah, a prophet, says, “Because you have allied yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works.” The reason he names is the alliance with Ahaziah, king of Israel, who acted wickedly.

explanations.answer: Jehoshaphat kept plunder from the battle
explanations.explanation: Plunder isn't what Eliezer brings up. Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah, a prophet, says, “Because you have allied yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works.” That's the reason the text gives, and it has to do with Ahaziah, king of Israel.
